rem:torus-knot-shell-binding-interpretat:
Remark Torus-knot mediation of inter-shell crossings. Withdrawn. The shell-size rule used here, that a closing shell of size n_s is bound by the torus knot T_{2,n_s}, is withdrawn. Its basis was a mislabel: (\sigma_0\sigma_1)^2\sigma_0 closes to T(2,4), not to the cinquefoil T(2,5). The rule stays withdrawn until it is derived. The interpretation below describes the withdrawn proposal.

When a nuclear shell closes (indicated by a palindromic Poincaré histogram), the next nucleon cannot enter the closed shell. It must start a new shell. The inter-shell crossing is mediated by a torus knot operator T_{2,k} whose index k equals the size of the closed shell. This proposition formalizes the inductive construction across shell boundaries and derives the magic numbers from the torus knot hierarchy.
rem:hopf-link-non-magic:
Remark Hopf link as the canonical non-magic knot operator (lowest cohomological degree). Hopf link as the simplest knot operator. The Hopf link T_{2,2} is the simplest non-trivial 2-component link in the framework's knot-operator basis:

  • Crossing number 2 (minimum for any non-trivial link).
  • Hyperbolic volume 0 (Seifert-fibered, not hyperbolic).
  • Complement S^3 \setminus \mathrm{Hopf} \simeq T^2 — cohomology rank \leq 2 in every degree.
  • Multivariable Alexander polynomial \Delta(t_1, t_2) = 1 (the standard convention for 2-component links is the multivariable form; the single-variable \Delta(t) = 0 for the Hopf link in the literature should not be confused with this). In the QOU framework's reading the Hopf link is the cohomologically minimal non-trivial link — its Alexander structure carries no signed information, which is the link-theoretic fact behind its E^{0, *}-only cohomological location.
  • Fundamental group: \mathbb{Z} \oplus \mathbb{Z} — abelian.

Cohomological location in the framework. The Hopf link lives entirely in the E_\infty^{0, *} slot of the brane-tower spectral sequence (conj:mass-endomorphism) — the descended Markov-trace piece.

Non-magic shells use the Hopf link. At non-magic n at substrate q_0, the SDP optimum T^*(n, q_0) is Hopf-decomposable, expressible as a tensor product of Hopf links and trivial ribbons. It lives entirely in E_\infty^{0, *} (the descended Markov-trace piece per Mass endomorphism conjecture).

Magic shells require higher-cohomology operators. At magic n, the SDP optimum requires non-trivial contribution from E_\infty^{p, q \geq 1} — operators NOT Hopf-decomposable. The torus-knot shell-binding proposition proposed that the active operator at each magic n is one of the six Bring-embeddable torus knots \{T_{2,3}, T_{2,5}, T_{2,7}, T_{2,9}, T_{3,4}, T_{3,5}\}, none of which is Hopf-decomposable. Its shell-size rule T_{2,n_s} is withdrawn, so that proposition does not establish which operator is active at a magic n.

Operational reading of the magic predicate. Selection of the active knot operator at strand count n is a topological-class decision:

n class Active knot operator Cohomological grading
non-magic Hopf-decomposable (e.g. T_{2,2}^{\otimes k}) E_\infty^{0, *}
magic non-Hopf Bring torus knot (T_{p, q} with q \geq 3, p \in \{2, 3\}) E_\infty^{p \geq 1, q \geq 1}

This matches the empirical mass-decomposition observation (conj:mass-endomorphism) that descended \mathrm{tr}_M contributes \lesssim 0.5\% of magic-shell binding; the rest is brane-tower (= higher-cohomological) contribution.

cor:spectral-decomposition-qvalue:
Corollary Spectral decomposition of the \mathcal{Q}_q-value over the torus knot basis of \Sigma_4. This is a direct consequence of the cohomological embedding (completeness of the torus knot basis on \Sigma_g) applied to the beta decay transfer matrix.

Let \Sigma_g be a genus-g surface and \mathcal{E}_g = \{\tau(r,s) : \tfrac{(r-1)(s-1)}{2} \leq g\} the set of torus knot labels embeddable on \Sigma_g. For \beta^- decay \mathcal{N}_{Z,N} \to \mathcal{N}_{Z+1,N-1}, the Q-value admits the spectral decomposition:

  Q
  = 
  \underbrace{
    \Bigl|\log_q\frac{P_{\mathrm{dau}}(q)}{P_{\mathrm{par}}(q)}\Bigr|
    \cdot \hbar_q \cdot \frac{m_e}{3}
  }_{\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{bare}}}
   \times 
  \underbrace{
    \prod_{\tau(r,s) \in \mathcal{E}_g}
    F\!\bigl(\tau(r,s), N\bigr)
  }_{\displaystyle\text{knot operator product}},

where:

(i) P(q) = \prod_{j=0}^{A-2} \hat{V}_j(q) is the Skein polynomial from the inductive chain construction (transfer matrix). Each chain \hat{V}_j = z \cdot M_j[0][0] + M_j[1][0] (with Markov parameter z = q^3/(q^2+1) \approx 0.612688037 at q_0) is pre-reduced via the 2\!\times\!2 matrix recurrence. This requires zero Hecke steps. It ensures \mathcal{N}_{Z,N} is in Gröbner--Shirshov normal form at every inductive stage.

At z = q^3/(q^2+1), each transfer-matrix factor \hat{V}_j and hence P(q) has coefficients in \mathbb{Q}(q) with no half-integer powers of q; the numerical evaluations of \mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{bare}} are tabulated in the interpretation.

(ii) \log_q(x) = \ln x / \ln q is the q-natural logarithm. It counts exceptional divisor levels along the color tube fiber of \Sigma_g. The constant \hbar_q = (q - 1)/q is the quantum Planck constant. This is the action per divisor step. The factor m_e/3 is the mass per crossing of the electron word \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0 (electron), which has 3 letters. (The backup trefoil electron \mathcal{K}_{\tau(2,3)} also has 3 crossings, so the factor is the same in both readings.) The product \hbar_q \cdot m_e / 3 replaces the intermediate notation \mathfrak{E}_{\mathrm{int}} \cdot \mu_0. These cancel algebraically.

(iii) F(\tau(r,s), N) is the knot operator of \tau(r,s) acting on the converting neutron's shell:

  F(\tau(r,s), N)
  = 
  \begin{cases}
    1
    & \tau(r,s) \notin \mathcal{E}_g
     \text{ (null: zero action on \(\Sigma_g\))} \\[4pt]
    1
    & \text{shell unchanged by decay (cancels in ratio)} \\[4pt]
    \mathrm{tr}_M\!\bigl(
      \tau(r,s) \cdot T_{\beta\text{-decay}}(q)
    \bigr)
    & \text{active shell, partially filled} \\[4pt]
    \dfrac{\bigl|\mathrm{tr}_M\!\bigl(
      e_{(1^3)} \cdot \tau(r,s) \cdot
      T_{\beta\text{-decay}}(q) \cdot e_{(1^3)}
    \bigr)\bigr|}{\bigl|\mathrm{tr}_M\!\bigl(T_{\beta\text{-decay}}(q)\bigr)\bigr|}
    & \text{active shell, fully filled (Pauli)}
  \end{cases}

with T_{\beta\text{-decay}}(q) = \sigma_0 \sigma_1^{-1} \in H_3(q) the beta decay operator (beta decay), and e_{(1^3)} the alternating Young symmetrizer of H_3(q) (glossary).

At z = q^3/(q^2+1) the fourth case is degenerate: the Ocneanu weight of every partition with three rows vanishes, so \mathrm{tr}_M\bigl(e_{(1^3)} \cdot x \cdot e_{(1^3)}\bigr) = 0 for every x \in H_3(q), and the fully filled branch returns F = 0 and hence Q = 0 on every magic-number shell; no non-vanishing replacement projection has yet been derived. The corollary is therefore asserted only for decays whose converting shell is not fully filled. The fully filled (magic-number) case is excluded from its scope, because on that case the formula returns Q = 0, which is not a Q-value.

(iv) The product over \mathcal{E}_g collapses to a single term. Only the converting neutron's shell knot \tau(k^*) is active. All other shells cancel between parent and daughter. Non-embeddable knots contribute F = 1.

(v) On the scope fixed in (iii), the decomposition is exact. The embeddable torus knots form a complete basis for the representation ring of H_n(q) restricted to \Sigma_g, by the self-duality \tau(r,s) \leftrightarrow \tau(s,r) and the Rosso–Jones completeness of torus knot invariants (cohomological embedding). No higher-order corrections exist; the tower terminates definitively at degree \lfloor 2g/(g-1) \rfloor.

prf:spectral-decomposition-qvalue:
Proof Proof of spectral decomposition qvalue. Sketch.

  1. Completeness. The Rosso–Jones formula decomposes J_{\tau(r,s)}(q) = \sum_{\lambda \vdash r} d_\lambda(q) \cdot \omega_\lambda^s into irreps of H_r(q). Every irrep \lambda is recoverable from the torus knot data by Möbius inversion on the power sums \omega^s. The self-duality \tau(r,s) \leftrightarrow \tau(s,r) provides the required inner product. Thus, \mathcal{E}_g spans the representation ring at each degree \leq \lfloor 2g/(g-1) \rfloor.

  2. Inductive chain construction. Each nucleon k is added by extending the 2\!\times\!2 chain matrices: M_j \leftarrow M_j \cdot T_{j {}^j\!\bowtie_k k}(q) for existing positions j < k, and M_{k-1} = T_{(k\!-\!1) {}^{k-1}\!\bowtie_k k}(q) for the new position. The Hecke reduction \sigma^2 = (q - q^{-1})\sigma + 1 acts strictly within each 2\!\times\!2 chain. This demands zero Yang–Baxter steps and zero Hecke steps on the multi-generator element. The nuclear word \mathcal{N}_{Z,N} = \prod_j (\mathfrak{w}^+_j \sigma_j + \mathfrak{w}^0_j) employs distinct generators, ensuring it remains in Gröbner--Shirshov normal form.

  3. Shell cancellation. The parent and daughter nuclei share all chains except those traversing the converting nucleon. The log ratio \log_q(P_{\mathrm{dau}}/P_{\mathrm{par}}) = \sum_j [\log_q \hat{V}_j^{\mathrm{dau}} - \log_q \hat{V}_j^{\mathrm{par}}] therefore accumulates contributions only from generators j that explicitly interact with the converting nucleon.

  4. Pauli projection. A fully occupied shell of n fermions is completely antisymmetric. Under the Schur–Weyl decomposition of H_3(q), the decay operator T_{\beta\text{-decay}}(q) projects onto the alternating irrep (1^3) via e_{(1^3)} \cdot T_{\beta\text{-decay}}(q) \cdot e_{(1^3)}. The symmetric and standard irreps cancel entirely in the fully occupied state.

  5. Tower termination. The degree-k tower knot \tau(r, s^k) demands genus (r-1)(s^k - 1)/2. For g = 4: degree 1 admits 4 knots, degree 2 admits 2 knots (\tau(2,9) and \tau(3,4)), and degree 3 requires genus \geq 13. Consequently, the jet bundle over \Sigma_4 possesses exactly three non-zero levels (k = 0, 1, 2).

Degree-1 knots are already encoded in \mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{bare}} through distinct vertex weights (\mathfrak{p} {}^i\!\oplus_j \mathfrak{p}, \mathfrak{n} {}^i\!\oplus_j \mathfrak{n}, \mathfrak{p} {}^i\!\oplus_j \mathfrak{n} — inter-particle Hopf links with crossing indices i, j), so F = 1 for shells 1–4. The active correction comes from degree-2 knots only.

rem:rj-inner-product-interpretation:
Remark The Rosso--Jones inner product as archimedean descent of the categorical trace. The Rosso--Jones inner product \langle -, - \rangle_{\mathrm{RJ}} (canonical inner product) is the archimedean descent of the categorical trace \mathrm{tr} \colon \mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(A) \to R to the Iwahori--Hecke subalgebra.

The chain of identifications is:

Level Object Role
Categorical \mathrm{tr} = \mathrm{ev}_A \circ (\mathrm{id}_{A^\vee} \otimes -) \circ \mathrm{coev}_A Integration in the action \mathfrak{S}_q = \mathrm{tr}(\mathcal{L}_q)
Archimedean Markov trace \mathrm{tr}_M on H_r(q) Descent of \mathrm{tr} to the Hecke algebra
Representation ring \langle -, - \rangle_{\mathrm{RJ}} = \sum_\lambda d_\lambda(q) \cdot \mathrm{tr}_\lambda(-) \cdot \mathrm{tr}_\lambda(-) Diagonal form via Schur orthogonality
Q-value F_{\mathrm{deg2}} = \sum_\tau J(\tau) \cdot \mathrm{tr}_M(\tau \cdot \Delta_\beta) / \sum_\tau J(\tau) \cdot \mathrm{tr}_M(\Delta_\beta) RJ-weighted spectral projection

The categorical action (canonical action) integrates the Lagrangian via \mathrm{tr}. In the archimedean realization, this becomes the Markov trace on the Hecke algebra. The Markov trace decomposes via Schur orthogonality into quantum-dimension weights d_\lambda(q). These are the Rosso--Jones weights. The shell correction F_{\mathrm{deg2}} in the Q-value formula (spectral decomposition) uses exactly this inner product to weight the degree-2 torus knots \tau(2,9) and \tau(3,4).

Schur orthogonality leaves no freedom in the weighting (Proposition (ii)). The quantum dimensions are determined by q alone.

sec:atomic-shells-element-instances-prea:
Applying the shell-construction rules and the Rumer–Jones inner product element-by-element across Z \ge 1 generates the electronic configurations of the periodic table from pure braid topology:

  • Helium and the noble-gas closures: Paired electron strands linked as a closed Hopf configuration saturate the 1s^2 shell, and the noble-gas characterization theorem proves that full torus-knot closures at Z \in \{2, 10, 18, 36, 54, 86\} maximize ionization energy while driving electron affinity to zero.
  • Alkali metals and metallic character: A single unpaired strand outside a closed torus-knot core defines the metallic character invariant, reaching its extremal value at francium (Z = 87).
  • Hydrogen orbital writhe: Explicit writhe and crossing tables for the Z = 1 hydrogenic orbitals (1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 3d) anchor the atomic spectrum for the subsequent transcendence analysis.
rem:electron-shells-hopf:
Remark Electron shells as closed sub-Hopf links of the electron chain. The electron configuration of atoms is derived from the closed sub-Hopf link structure of the multi-electron chain. This yields the shell capacities 2, 8, 18, 32, \ldots = 2n^2.

The electron link.

A neutral atom with Z protons binds Z electrons, each the word e^- = \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0. The stable atom takes the form:

  \mathcal{A}(p, n)
  = 
  \underbrace{Z\mathfrak{p} \oplus N\mathfrak{n}}_{\text{nucleus}}
   \oplus 
  \underbrace{p \cdot e^-}_{\text{electron cloud}}.

The electron cloud p \cdot e^- forms a chain of p electrons bound by Hopf links. An electron shell defines a maximal closed sub-Hopf link of this chain. It forms a subset S of electrons such that \bigbowtie_{i \in S} e^-_i splits from the remaining chain. Each electron is the word e^- = \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0 \in B_3 (electron knot), and its closure is itself a Hopf link with two components. So a sub-Hopf link here counts electrons, not link components, and the linking number between two electrons needs a choice of one component of each. That choice is not fixed in the corpus.

First example: helium (p = 2, n = 2).

The helium electron cloud e^- \oplus e^- forms a Hopf link of two electrons. This pair acts as a closed sub-link. It rejects a third electron unless the linking number increases. The two electrons fill the 1s shell.

Topological closure makes helium a noble gas. A third electron (lithium) forces a new sub-link. This weakly couples to the first to form the 2s shell.

Shell capacities from sub-link closure.

The conjecture is that the maximum number of electrons in a closed sub-Hopf link at level n fixes the shell capacity at 2n^2. A rigorous derivation remains open:

Shell n Capacity 2n^2 Cumulative Pure-2n^2 closure Closed sub-link
1 2 2 He (= noble) e^- \oplus e^-
2 8 10 Ne (= noble) 8 \cdot e^- (Hopf 8-chain)
3 18 28 Ni (not noble) 18 \cdot e^-
4 32 60 Nd (not noble) 32 \cdot e^-

Caveat — the pure-2n^2 closures are not the chemical noble gases. The cumulative pure-2n^2 count [2, 10, 28, 60, \ldots] maps the closed-shell sequence of a pure-Coulomb atom. The chemical noble gases [2, 10, 18, 36, 54, 86] follow the Madelung / n+\ell (Aufbau) ordering driven by electron–electron screening. The two sequences match only at He and Ne. They diverge at n = 3. Reproducing the physical noble gases requires both the 2n^2 derivation and a categorical screening mechanism. The noble-gas identifications are stated as a target.

The noble gases (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn) define atoms whose electron cloud reduces to a union of closed sub-links. Every electron belongs to a complete shell.

Photon absorption as a knot operation.

A photon absorption event promotes a single electron between sub-Hopf links. The knot picture models this process:

  1. Incoming photon: A wavefront (wavefront propagation) carries energy E = h\nu specified by the categorical Lagrangian (categorical Lagrangian).
  2. Absorption: The photon adds a strand-adding curl to the electron word, e_n \mapsto e_n\sigma_{n+1}. This is a Markov stabilisation, so the closure stays the Hopf link while the strand level rises by one. How this curl moves the electron to an outer sub-link is not re-derived.
  3. Emission: The electron decays. The curl is removed. The system re-emits a photon of identical energy.

Curls that preserve the topological type of the remaining sub-links dictate the selection rules.

Maximal shell number from stability.

The stability of the electron–hadron interaction bounds the number of electron shells. The outermost electron must remain Hopf-linked to the nucleus. Fluid dynamics models this via the vortex capture radius.

The ionization energy of the outermost electron scales as:

  E_{\mathrm{ion}}  \propto 
  \frac{\mathfrak{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}(\text{electron--nucleus link})}{n^2}

where n denotes the shell number. The atom ionizes when E_{\mathrm{ion}} drops below the thermal energy k_B T. This threshold sets a maximum shell number n_{\max} determined by the nuclear charge p and the ambient temperature.

Open problems.

  1. Shell capacity derivation: Prove that the maximum number of electrons in a closed sub-Hopf link at level n strictly equals 2n^2.
  2. Photon energy: Derive the photon energy E = h\nu from the categorical action. The wavefront equation supplies propagation. The frequency \nu should match the winding number of the wavefront around the Reeb flow.
  3. Selection rules: Identify the permitted Skein operations on the electron link. These recover the dipole selection rules \Delta \ell = \pm 1.
  4. Orbital shapes: Match electron orbitals to the topological types of the sub-Hopf link. The angular momentum quantum number \ell acts as the Seifert surface genus.
  5. Noble gas stability: Prove that atoms whose electron cloud decomposes into a union of closed sub-links achieve maximal ionization energy in each period. The crossing energy of a complete sub-link must represent a local maximum.
rem:helium-hopf-diagram:
Remark Helium: two electrons forming a closed Hopf link. The helium atom \mathcal{A}(2, 2) provides the simplest closed electron shell. Its electron cloud comprises two electrons e^- = \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0 (electron knot) joined by a Hopf link \mathcal{L}_H.

\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=3em, column sep=4em]
  & \boxed{\mathcal{N}(2{,}2)} \ar[dl, "\oplus"', dashed] \ar[dr, "\oplus", dashed] & \\
  e^- \ar[rr, "\mathcal{L}_H"', "\text{Hopf link}", bend right=15]
  & & e^- \\
  \underset{e_1}{\text{electron 1}} & \underset{1s^2 \text{ (closed)}}{\text{—————————————}} & \underset{e_2}{\text{electron 2}}
\end{tikzcd}

The Hopf link \mathcal{L}_H defines the linking operation between e_1 and e_2. Each electron threads the Seifert surface of the other exactly once (\mathrm{lk}(e_1, e_2) = 1). The closure of each electron is itself a two-component Hopf link, so this linking number is taken between one chosen component of each; which component is not fixed in the corpus.

Full atom structure.

  \mathcal{A}(2, 2) = 
  \underbrace{2\mathfrak{p} \oplus 2\mathfrak{n}}_{\alpha\text{-particle}}
   \oplus 
  \underbrace{e^- \oplus e^-}_{1s^2\text{ shell (closed)}}

Closure of the shell.

The linking matrix of the two-electron Hopf link is:

  L =  \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.

This matrix has rank 2. Adding a third component e_3 requires \mathrm{lk}(e_3, e_1) \geq 1 and \mathrm{lk}(e_3, e_2) \geq 1. This increases the total linking number from 1 to at least 3. The crossing energy cost of these extra links exceeds the binding energy gain. The atom expels the third electron to a higher shell.

Comparison: lithium (p = 3, n = 4).

\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em]
  & \boxed{\mathcal{N}(3{,}4)} \ar[d, "\oplus"', dashed] & \\
  & \underset{1s^2}{\bigl(e^- \oplus e^-\bigr)} \ar[d, "\oplus"', dashed, "\text{level 2}"] & \\
  & e^- & \\
  & \underset{2s^1}{\text{outer electron}} &
\end{tikzcd}

  \mathcal{A}(3, 4) = 
  3\mathfrak{p} \oplus 4\mathfrak{n}
   \oplus 
  \underbrace{(e^- \oplus e^-)}_{1s^2}
   \oplus 
  \underbrace{e^-}_{2s^1}

The third electron links to the closed 1s^2 sub-link at a higher linking level. It passes around the entire Hopf pair instead of threading through it. This forms the 2s shell. The electron links to the 1s^2 cluster as a single unit.
prop:noble-gas-characterization:
Proposition Noble gas characterization: a full shell has no free linking site. An atom \mathcal{A}(p,n) constitutes a noble gas if and only if its electron cloud p \cdot e^- decomposes into a disjoint union of closed sub-Hopf links. Every shell has no free linking site.

Statement. Let \mathcal{A}(p,n) be a stable atom with electron cloud \mathcal{E} = p \cdot e^-. The atom \mathcal{A} is chemically inert (noble) if and only if a partition

  \mathcal{E} = S_1 \sqcup S_2 \sqcup \cdots \sqcup S_k

exists satisfying:

  1. Closure: Each S_i = 2n_i^2 \cdot e^- forms a closed sub-Hopf link at level n_i. The electron chain within S_i admits no additional linking without increasing total linking number.
  2. Exhaustion: Every electron belongs to an S_i. No unlinked electrons remain.
  3. Monotone nesting: The sequence n_1 < n_2 < \cdots < n_k holds. The linking of S_{i+1} threads through S_i without disrupting its closure.

Cumulative shell closure characterizes the six noble gases:

See Table.
rem:noble-gas-ionization-affinity: Remark Ionization energy and electron affinity of the noble gases.
prf:noble-gas-characterization:
Proof Proof of noble gas characterization. Sketch.

The forward direction (closed partition implies inertness) follows from the Hopf stability proposition. A closed sub-Hopf link remains stable under small perturbations of the linking matrix. No single crossing change can open or close a linking site.

The reverse direction (inertness implies closed partition) follows from the shell conjecture. If the electron cloud is not a union of closed sub-links, then at least one electron contains an available linking site. The atom lowers its energy by capturing an additional electron, contradicting chemical inertness.
rem:noble-gas-characterization-interpret:

This yields:

Full shell = no free linking site.

A shell fills by exhausting available linking sites at its level, not by reaching a numerical threshold. Topological rigidity drives inertness. No crossing remains available for a new electron.

Remark (mathematical novelty). This topological characterization replaces heuristic chemistry with a rigid sub-Hopf link invariant. It formally binds empirical ionization energy peaks to crossing-energy maxima.

prop:metallic-character-knot:
Proposition Metallic character from incomplete sub-Hopf links. Statement. Let \mathcal{A}(p,n) be a stable atom whose electron cloud decomposes as

\mathcal{E} = p \cdot e^- = S_1 \sqcup \cdots \sqcup S_k \sqcup R,

where each S_i is a closed sub-Hopf link and R is the residual sub-link. The atom \mathcal{A} exhibits metallic character if and only if:

  1. Incompleteness: |R| < 2n_{k+1}^2. The outermost sub-link contains unfilled linking sites.
  2. Low crossing energy: \mathfrak{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}(R) \ll \mathfrak{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}(S_k). The outermost electrons link loosely relative to the inner closed shells.
  3. Site availability: R contains at least one open linking site. The atom permits Hopf linking to an adjacent residual sub-link without disrupting the closed inner shells S_i.
rem:metallic-character-knot-interpretati:
Remark Metallic bonding, conduction, and the residual linking number \lambda(R). Noble gases possess closed sub-Hopf links. Metals possess an incomplete outermost sub-Hopf link with low crossing energy. This allows neighbouring atoms to share sites.

Metallic bonding. In a metallic lattice, adjacent residual sub-links R_a and R_b merge their open linking sites. Outermost electrons Hopf-link to the neighbour offering the lowest crossing energy. This models electron delocalisation:

  R_a \oplus R_b
   \leadsto 
  \text{shared sub-link } R_{ab}
  = 
  R_a \cup R_b \text{ with merged linking sites.}

Delocalised electrons form a lattice-spanning sub-Hopf chain. This acts as a conduction band. Electrons slide along this chain via Reidemeister II moves. These crossing exchanges conserve the total linking number.

Strategy. Macroscopic properties translate into structural conditions on sub-Hopf links. Macroscopic conductivity corresponds to Reidemeister II mobility. Shared bonding becomes merged linking sites. Energetic inequalities derive from crossing energies, parametrized by the residual index \lambda(R).

Classification. The residual sub-link size |R| and shell capacity 2n_{k+1}^2 govern metallic behaviour.

\lvert R\rvert vs. capacity Character Examples
\lvert R\rvert = 1 Strong metal (alkalis) Li, Na, K
\lvert R\rvert = 2 Strong metal (alkaline earths) Mg, Ca, Sr
\lvert R\rvert \approx \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot 2n^2 Transition metal Fe, Cu, Ni
\lvert R\rvert = 2n^2 - 1 Weak nonmetal (halogens) F, Cl, Br
\lvert R\rvert = 2n^2 Noble gas (no residual) He, Ne, Ar

Alkali metals (|R| = 1) contain one loose electron. The minimal crossing energy to detach this electron matches their low ionization energy and high reactivity.

Transition metals have partially filled d-sub-links. These have \ell = 2, Seifert genus 2, and 10 linking sites. For |R_d| between 1 and 9, multiple open sites exist at similar crossing energies. This yields:

  • Variable oxidation states: Electrons detach or share at similar energy costs.
  • Catalytic activity: Open d-sites temporarily Hopf-link to substrate electrons.
  • Magnetic behaviour: Unpaired electrons carry uncompensated writhe (+3 each), producing a net magnetic moment.

Conductivity. Electrical conductivity requires electron mobility along the lattice-spanning chain. An external field biases Reidemeister II moves. This produces a net drift of electrons.

Resistance arises from pinning sites. These local energy barriers impede crossing exchanges. The barriers derive from:

  • Lattice defects that disrupt chain topology.
  • Thermal fluctuations that induce transient Reidemeister I moves.
  • Phonons that modulate crossing energies via periodic compressions.

Low temperatures minimize crossing disruptions and lower resistance.

Residual linking number. Noble gases have R = \varnothing. They lack residual sub-links, open linking sites, and delocalisation. The residual linking number \lambda(R) parametrizes the chemical spectrum:

  \lambda(R) = 0 \Longleftrightarrow \text{noble gas},
  \qquad
  \lambda(R) > 0 \Longleftrightarrow \text{non-inert}.

Metallic character is strongest when \lambda(R) is small relative to shell capacity. It weakens as \lambda(R) approaches the closure threshold 2n^2.
rem:metallic-character-knot-novelty: Remark Mathematical novelty of the residual-linking-number metallic classification. The residual linking number \lambda(R) provides a knot-theoretic metric for metallic character. This formalizes conductivity via Reidemeister transport. A rigid topological invariant replaces qualitative chemical models.
rem:francium-extremal-metal:
Remark Francium: the most metallic element as a single loose electron. Metallic character strengthens as the residual sub-link R shrinks and the shell number n grows. Francium (p = 87) extremises both conditions.

Francium's electron cloud. Francium partitions its 87 electrons as:

  \mathcal{E}(87)
  = 
  \underbrace{S_1 \sqcup S_2 \sqcup \cdots \sqcup S_6}_{86
  \text{ electrons in closed sub-links (radon core)}}
  \sqcup
  \underbrace{R}_{|R| = 1}.

The inner 86 electrons form the radon core. These six fully closed sub-Hopf links interlock every electron. The 87th electron sits alone in shell n = 7. This single loose electron weakly Hopf-links to the core.

Extremality of francium. Francium minimises the outermost crossing energy in two ways:

  1. Minimal residual: |R| = 1. The lone electron lacks an interlocking partner. It occupies an open linking site without compensating closure. Elements with |R| \geq 2 exhibit partial interlocking among residual electrons. This raises detachment energy.
  2. Maximal shell depth: n = 7. The crossing energy scales as \mathfrak{E}_{\mathrm{cross}} \propto 1/n^2. The n = 7 electron is the most weakly bound alkali electron.

Consequently, francium exhibits:

  • A low ionization energy (E_{\mathrm{ion}} \approx 4.07 \mathrm{eV}), though caesium is lower (see the table).
  • The highest electropositive character. It donates its lone electron readily.
  • The strongest metallic bonding tendency. Its single open linking site couples to neighbours with negligible crossing cost.

The alkali series. The alkali metals possess |R| = 1 at increasing shell depth:

See Table.

Each atom has one loose electron. The crossing energy decreases monotonically with n. The slight ionization-energy uptick for francium reflects relativistic contraction of the 7s orbital. This corresponds to a tightening of the Hopf linking to the Borromean core at high p.

Dual extremum: fluorine. Fluorine (p = 9) anchors the opposite end of the spectrum. It holds |R| = 7 electrons out of a shell-2 capacity of 8. The residual sub-link sits one electron short of closure. This empty linking site makes fluorine the most electronegative element. It pulls an electron from any neighbour to close its sub-link. This action is the topological dual to francium donating an electron.

  \underbrace{\text{Fr}: |R| = 1}_{\text{most metallic}}
  \qquad\longleftrightarrow\qquad
  \underbrace{\text{F}: |R| = 2n^2 - 1}_{\text{most nonmetallic}}

The filling fraction |R| / 2n^2 of the outermost sub-Hopf link parametrises the entire metallic–nonmetallic spectrum.

conj:hydrogen-shell-writhe:
Conjecture Electron shell number from the writhe of the level word. Proposition (conditional on Quarks as Borromean-linked unknots in the exceptional divisor). Let e^- = \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0 \in B_3 be the electron word (electron knot), whose closure is the Hopf link, Hopf-linked to a proton anchor. For n \geq 1 let the level-n word be

  e_n = \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0\,\sigma_2\sigma_3\cdots\sigma_n \in B_{n+2},
  \qquad e_1 = e^-,

obtained from e^- by n - 1 strand-adding curls. Let w be the writhe (exponent sum) of e_n.

  1. Shell--writhe correspondence. Each curl appends the next generator, which is a Markov stabilisation, so the closure of e_n remains the positive Hopf link T(2,2). The writhe of e_n is w = n + 2, so the shell level is n = w - 2, with ground state w = 3 (n = 1).
  2. Orbital counting (open on the two-component closure). The count \sum_{\ell=0}^{n-1}(2\ell + 1) = n^2 of the normal-bundle orbital space is formulated for the resonance modes of a single-component trefoil T_{2,3} in its normal bundle. Because the closure of e_n has two components (T(2,2)), a corresponding two-component normal-bundle construction remains open.
  3. Energy scaling (open on the two-component closure). Likewise, the Seifert-surface-area derivation of E_n = -E_{\mathrm{ion}}/n^2 in the single-component trefoil model has not yet been extended to the two-component Hopf-link closure of e_n.

Single-component trefoil model. In the alternative model where the shell-n electron is the two-strand word \sigma_0^{2n+1} \in B_2 (closing to T_{2,2n+1}, with ground state T_{2,3}), the shell number is n = (w - 1)/2 with w = 2n + 1. The two models agree at the ground state w = 3, n = 1 and diverge for n \geq 2.

Archimedean specialisation. What follows evaluates generic q-deformation identities at the real-valued substrate parameter q_0. The categorical identities remain valid over any abstract coefficient ring.
rem:hydrogen-orbitals:
Remark Hydrogen orbitals: the electron word around the Borromean anchor. The picture.

Hydrogen couples an electron to a small Borromean proton. The proton occupies the center as a compact \mathcal{B}_3 formed of three unknots with \mathrm{Vol} \approx 7.328. The electron is the word e^- = \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0 \in B_3 (electron knot), whose closure is the Hopf link. It loops around the proton and Hopf-links to it.

\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=4em, column sep=5em]
  & \underset{\text{\normalsize electron } e^- = \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0}{\bigcirc\!\!\!\bigcirc}
    \ar[d, "\oplus"', "\text{Hopf}", dashed] & \\
  & \underset{\text{\normalsize small } \mathcal{B}_3}{\bullet}
    & \\
  & \underset{\text{proton (anchor)}}{\mathrm{Vol} \approx 7.328} &
\end{tikzcd}

The Borromean volume pins the massive proton in place. The Hopf link has no hyperbolic volume. The electron mass m_e is the CAL-1 input, not derived here. The Hopf link \oplus provides the electromagnetic binding.

Shell transitions as strand-adding curls.

The ground state is e_1 = e^- = \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0, with writhe w = 3. Photon absorption is the strand-adding curl: it appends the next generator,

  e_n = \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0\,\sigma_2\cdots\sigma_n \in B_{n+2}
  \;\longmapsto\;
  e_{n+1} = e_n\,\sigma_{n+1} \in B_{n+3}.

Appending \sigma_{n+1} is a Markov stabilisation, so the closure stays the Hopf link. The word stays Gröbner–Shirshov reduced, and the level shows as its length. Each curl raises the writhe by 1:

  n \to n + 1
  \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
  w \to w + 1,
  \qquad\text{so}\qquad
  n = w - 2 = 1, 2, 3, \ldots
  \quad\text{for}\quad w = 3, 4, 5, \ldots

This is item 1 of the shell--writhe correspondence. Where the added curls sit in the brane tower is not re-derived for the ruled electron.

Backup reading. If the electron is the trefoil \sigma_0^3 \in B_2, a level step adds two Reidemeister I curls on the same strand, w \to w + 2, and n = (w - 1)/2. That reading puts the ground state (w = 3) in the base space \mathcal{S}_0 and the extra curls of w = 5 in the blow-up \mathcal{S}_1. The sub-shell count below is also built on it.

Sub-shells from resonance modes (backup reading).

This count has not been re-derived for the ruled electron. Its closure has two components, and no counterpart of the trefoil normal-bundle construction below is on record for it.

The embedded backup trefoil T_{2,3} vibrates transversely within its normal bundle N_{T_{2,3}} in the Bring surface. Laplacian eigenvalues on the trefoil curve govern the resonance frequencies. The mode integers \ell = 0, 1, 2, \ldots label the standing-wave patterns:

  • Mode \ell = 0: Uniform (no oscillation) — the s orbital.
  • Mode \ell = 1: One wavelength around the curve — the p orbital.
  • Mode \ell = 2: Two wavelengths — the d orbital.

At linking level n, the Seifert surface has effective length proportional to n. Only modes with wavelength \geq L/n fit. This yields the cutoff \ell = 0, 1, \ldots, n - 1. Each mode \ell vibrates transversely in ambient 3-space. Projected onto the sphere, the 2\ell + 1 standing-wave orientations match the spherical harmonics Y_\ell^m. Thus:

  \sum_{\ell=0}^{n-1} (2\ell + 1) =  n^2
  \quad\text{orbitals per shell.}

This sum reproduces the observed capacity for all n.

Note on geometric counting.

The sum \sum(2\ell + 1) = n^2 matches standard quantum mechanics. The backup trefoil model identifies \ell with trefoil resonance modes and n with the writhe framing number. The remaining step requires a proof:

The space of sections of the normal bundle N_{T_{2,3}} of the trefoil in the Bring's surface, at total framing twist k = 2(n-1), has dimension n^2.

This is stated as The orbital space at shell n is the space of framing-k sections of the normal bundle in the Bring's-surface chapter.

The two ingredients of the count have different sources, and only one of them is representation-theoretic. The 2\ell + 1 orientations are the dimension of the irreducible \mathrm{SO}(3) representation V_\ell carried by the mode, matching the spherical harmonics Y_\ell^m. The cutoff \ell \leq n - 1 is not: it is the length-and-framing bound already used above, that only modes of wavelength at least L/n fit along the Seifert surface. In the eigenvalue form \lambda_\ell \leq \lambda_{n-1} this is an arithmetic consequence rather than a group-theoretic one, and it is proved with no symmetry group entering the argument.

For hydrogen (one electron), only the n = 1, \ell = 0 orbital is occupied in the ground state.

sec:topological-mass-formula-transcenden:
Through the archimedean realization \tau_{\mathrm{arch}}, the topological mass formula expresses particle mass ratios in terms of hyperbolic volumes \mathrm{Vol}(S^3 \setminus K) of link complements. By the Borel–Zagier theorem, hyperbolic volumes are periods of mixed Tate motives evaluated through the Bloch–Wigner dilogarithm D(z) at algebraic shape parameters z \in \overline{\mathbb{Q}} and are expected to be transcendental over \mathbb{Q}.

This section compiles the master knot-formula table across the particle spectrum, proves Chern–Simons evaluation faithfulness and its corollaries, formulates the single-volume irrationality conjecture (the weaker companion of the hyperbolic-volume transcendence conjecture stated with the topological mass formula), and establishes three-knot jet-order independence.
sec:hyperbolic-volumes-prose:
Hyperbolic volumes and the topological mass ansatz. Inertial mass originates in the topology of knot complements. The framework identifies every particle with a knot or link K (skein decomposition). Each knot carries a hyperbolic volume \mathrm{Vol}(K). This evaluates the volume of the complete hyperbolic metric on the complement S^3 \setminus K, computed via the Bloch--Wigner dilogarithm. Torus knots, such as the trefoil 3_1, have zero hyperbolic volume. Hyperbolic knots have positive volume.

The framework identifies the Higgs boson with the figure-eight knot 4_1 (cohomological embedding). Its volume is

  \mathrm{Vol}(4_1) = 2\,\mathrm{Cl}_2(\pi/3) = 6\,\Lambda(\pi/3)
    \approx 2.02988321281931,

where \mathrm{Cl}_2 denotes the Clausen function and \Lambda(\theta) = \mathrm{Cl}_2(2\theta)/2 the Lobachevsky function. The complement S^3 \setminus 4_1 decomposes into two regular ideal tetrahedra, each of volume \mathrm{Cl}_2(\pi/3) = 3\,\Lambda(\pi/3) \approx 1.01494.

The topological mass formula defines the mass \mathfrak{m}(K) of a particle with knot type K as

  \mathfrak{m}(K) =  \frac{\mathrm{Vol}(K)}{\hbar_q^{2}},
  \qquad
  \hbar_q  :=  1 - q^{-1}.

Here q > 1 represents the substrate parameter and \hbar_q represents the quantum planck constant. The mass functional \mathcal{M} is not additive for composite states. It satisfies a q-deformed Skein recursion at every crossing in the color-exchange diagram.
sec:descartes-intro: On Bring's genus-4 surface, the topological mass formula \mathfrak{m}(K) = \mathrm{Vol}(K)/\hbar_q^2 and the skein decomposition of the Jones polynomial unite the hyperbolic geometry of link complements with the Picard–Lefschetz thimbles of the exceptional colour tubes, providing the geometric invariants tabulated in the master knot-formula table below.
rem:knot-formula-table:
Remark Topological knot formulas for fundamental and composite particles. Introduce a compact notation to express the knot content of composite particles. A dictionary assigning elementary particles to knots has precedent in Avrin's model [avrin-2012], which reduces fermions and bosons, leptons and hadrons, to two knots on a torus, the unknot and the trefoil. The notation below takes only the idea of such a dictionary from that work; the knot assignments and the Hecke-algebra content are this paper's.

Compact notation.

See Table 1.

Derived shorthand for quarks. The up and down quarks are not independent generators. Each is an unknot strand of the Borromean braid \mathcal{B}_3 (up quark), distinguished by crossing orientation, and each has a lepton partner in the knot–particle dictionary:

  \mathfrak{u} \leftarrow  T_{2,3}, \qquad
  \mathfrak{d} \leftarrow  T_{2,3}^{\sigma}.

Here T_{2,3}^{\sigma} is the mirror trefoil T_{2,-3}; the mirror marks the down-type member of the doublet, not an antiparticle. The arrow names the lepton partner, not the quark's knot type. The heavier quarks follow a similar pattern: \mathfrak{s} \leftarrow T_{2,5}^{\sigma}, \mathfrak{c} \leftarrow T_{2,5}, \mathfrak{b} \leftarrow T_{2,7}^{\sigma}, \mathfrak{t} \leftarrow T_{3,4}.

Nucleon shorthand. The proton and neutron are color-tube-linked triples bound by Hopf links:

  \mathfrak{p} =  [\mathfrak{u}, \mathfrak{u}, \mathfrak{d}]_p \oplus \mathcal{L}_H,
  \qquad
  \mathfrak{n} =  [\mathfrak{u}, \mathfrak{d}, \mathfrak{d}]_p \oplus \mathcal{L}_H.

Nuclear composites. Nuclear composites are iterated Hopf linkings of nucleons. For a nucleus with Z protons and N neutrons:

  {}^A_Z\!\mathcal{K}
  = 
  \underbrace{\mathfrak{p} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathfrak{p}}_{Z}
   \oplus 
  \underbrace{\mathfrak{n} \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathfrak{n}}_{N}

where A = Z + N. A neutral atom appends Z electrons:

  {}^A_Z\!\mathcal{K}^0
  = 
  {}^A_Z\!\mathcal{K}
   \oplus 
  Z \cdot e^-.

This table lists each particle's knot content in the compact notation. The content is built from T_{m,n} generators via the three knot-particle generation operations. All entries satisfy the embeddability closure and descend to the base manifold.

See Table 3.

The Higgs field (mass mechanism) is the figure-eight knot 4_1 (\mathrm{Vol} = 2.0299, amphichiral: H = H^{\sigma}). The Higgs boson excitation (\approx 125 GeV) is the torus link T(2,8). This link is the unique genus-3 link spanning all three exceptional divisors on Bring's surface.
